name: Round City of Baghdad (Madinat al-Salam)
description: The circular core of Baghdad built by Caliph al-Mansur in 762–766 as the City of Peace, with four gates to Kufa, Damascus, Khurasan and Basra and the caliphal palace at its centre. Its remains lie under the modern city.

name: Khuld Palace (site)
description: A principal early Abbasid palace begun by al-Mansur in 773 between the Round City and the Tigris, with extensive gardens; its site is now occupied by modern buildings.

name: Taj Palace (site)
description: A caliphal palace begun by al-Mu‘tadid (892–902) on the Tigris in East Baghdad, the southern part of the Dar al-Khilafa palace complex after the capital returned from Samarra.

name: Al-‘Adudi Bimaristan (site)
description: One of the most advanced hospitals of the medieval Islamic world, founded by the Buyid ruler ‘Adud al-Dawla in West Baghdad shortly before his death in 983, and a centre of medical teaching.

name: Ctesiphon
description: The Parthian and Sasanian royal capital on the east bank of the Tigris 35 km south-east of Baghdad, capital of the Iranian empires for over 800 years until the Muslim conquest in 637.

name: Taq Kasra (Arch of Ctesiphon)
description: The great brick iwan that formed the façade of the main Sasanian palace at Ctesiphon, the only visible structure of the capital and a landmark in the history of vaulted architecture.

name: Seleucia on the Tigris
description: The first capital of the Seleucid Empire, founded about 305 BC on the west bank of the Tigris; it flourished under the Parthians and was destroyed by the Romans in AD 165.

name: Church of Kokhe
description: Ruins of the church at Kokhe, successor to Seleucia, seat of the Catholicos of the Church of the East from 310 to 780 and starting point of missions to Persia, India and China; around twenty patriarchal graves remain.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Church in Kokhe

approximateLocation: West bank of the Tigris, 32 km south of Baghdad

name: Dur-Kurigalzu (Aqar Quf)
description: A Kassite royal city founded by Kurigalzu I (d. c. 1375 BC) 30 km west of central Baghdad, whose ziggurat core still stands at Aqar Quf.

name: Sippar (Tell Abu Habbah)
description: A Sumerian and Babylonian city of the sun god Shamash on the Euphrates near Yusufiyah, 30 km south-west of Baghdad.

name: Sippar-Amnanum (Tell ed-Der)
description: Sippar’s sister city 6 km to the north-east, mainly developed in the Old Babylonian period.

name: Tell Harmal (Shaduppum)
description: An Old Babylonian administrative town of the kingdom of Eshnunna inside modern Baghdad, known for its tablets.

name: Tell Muhammad
description: An ancient mound on the Tigris near Tell Harmal, suggested as Diniktum.

name: Tell al-Dhiba‘i
description: A site in New Baghdad proposed as the Old Babylonian town of Uzarzalulu.

name: Bab al-Wastani
description: The only surviving gate of Baghdad’s eastern wall, built under Caliph al-Mustazhir (1094–1118), near the Suhrawardi mausoleum and the Wardiyya cemetery. It was restored in the 20th century and later housed military museums.
review_notes: Pin from an unlabelled Wikidata city-gate item next to the Suhrawardi mausoleum; confirm identity.

name: Talisman Gate (site)
description: A gate of the eastern wall described by Ibn Jubayr in 1185 and restored in 1220 by Caliph al-Nasir with decorative friezes and an inscription in his name. Murad IV bricked it up in 1638, and Ottoman troops destroyed it as they withdrew in 1917.

name: Bab al-Mu‘adham
description: One of four gates built under Caliph al-Mustarshid in the late Abbasid wall, later the Ottoman gate towards the Abu Hanifa mosque. The gate itself was demolished after 1917; the district between the Sarafiya and Sinak bridges keeps late-Ottoman and later buildings.
review_notes: Wikidata coordinates (33.315, 44.366) point to Karkh and were not used.

name: Abu Hanifa Mosque
description: The great mosque and shrine of A‘dhamiyya built around the tomb of Abu Hanifa, founder of the Hanafi school, rebuilt many times over the centuries.

name: Al-Kadhimiya Shrine
description: The shrine of the seventh and ninth Twelver Imams, Musa al-Kadhim and Muhammad al-Jawad, where Shaykh al-Mufid and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi are also buried.

name: Hadhrat al-Qadiriyya
description: The mausoleum, mosque and library of Abd al-Qadir al-Gilani, founder of the Qadiriyya Sufi order, in Bab al-Sheikh; the Qadiriyya library holds rare manuscripts.

name: Al-Khulafa Mosque and Suq al-Ghazl Minaret
description: Baghdad’s oldest surviving mosque site, first built in 908. Its Ilkhanid minaret, once the highest point of the city, survives beside a 1960s rebuilding.

name: Qamariyya Mosque
description: A late-Abbasid mosque on the Karkh bank of the Tigris, one of the oldest in Baghdad, renovated repeatedly but keeping its architectural character.

name: Zumurrud Khatun Mausoleum
description: The muqarnas-domed tomb of Zumurrud Khatun, wife of Caliph al-Mustadi and mother of al-Nasir, in the Sheikh Ma‘ruf cemetery; popularly called the tomb of Sitt Zubayda.

sources.sourceName: Wikipedia — Zumurrud Khatun Mosque and Mausoleum

name: Mausoleum of Umar al-Suhrawardi
description: The Abbasid-era conical muqarnas-domed tomb of Shihab al-Din Umar al-Suhrawardi, founder of the Suhrawardiyya order, near Bab al-Wastani.

name: Al-Musta‘sim Billah Mosque
description: A shrine-mosque in A‘dhamiyya, originally Mashhad al-Wu‘ud over the grave of Ahmad al-Sabti, son of Harun al-Rashid, which holds the tomb of the last Abbasid caliph, al-Musta‘sim.

name: Arif Agha Mosque (Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal)
description: A small Ottoman mosque with the mausoleum purported to hold Ahmad ibn Hanbal (780–855), moved there after a flood destroyed his original grave.

name: Buratha Mosque
description: A Twelver Shi‘i holy site in Karkh traditionally founded in the 7th century over a Nestorian monastery.

name: Mirjan Mosque (Madrasa al-Mirjaniyya)
description: The walled mosque of the madrasa founded in 1356 by the Jalayirid governor Amin al-Din Mirjan, with the tombs of scholars such as Nu‘man al-Alusi.

name: Al-Sarai Mosque
description: A mosque said to have been laid out by Caliph al-Nasir in 1193 near Bab al-Sultan, rebuilt by Hassan Pasha; the kings of Iraq prayed here in the royal era.

name: Al-Muradiyya Mosque
description: An early Ottoman mosque begun in 1566 by Murad Pasha on al-Maidan Square, whose minaret some consider the most beautiful in Baghdad.

name: Uzbek Mosque
description: A 17th-century mosque of Baghdad’s Uzbek community beside al-Maidan.

name: Mosque-Madrasa of al-Ahmadiyya
description: A mosque and madrasa built in 1796 by Ahmad al-Katkhuda, deputy of the Mamluk ruler Sulayman the Great, on al-Rashid Street at al-Maidan.

name: Haydar-Khana Mosque
description: A 19th-century mosque and madrasa by the Mamluk governor Dawud Pasha on a 12th-century mosque of Caliph al-Nasir; a forum of anti-British agitation in 1920.

name: Adila Khatun Mosque
description: A mosque founded by Adila Khatun, daughter of the Mamluk ruler Ahmad Pasha, near the Sarafiya bridge.

name: Al-Khilani Mosque
description: A Shi‘i mosque with an old shrine of disputed identity, once in the vanished Khilani cemetery; first recorded in 1726.

name: Siraj al-Din Mosque
description: A mosque of the Mamluk period under Hassan Pasha that names the Siraj al-Din quarter near the Qadiriyya shrine.

name: Sayyid Sultan Ali Mosque
description: A mosque, madrasa and mausoleum on al-Rashid Street, headquarters of the Rifa‘i Sufi order in Baghdad, around a tomb of disputed identity.

name: Shabandar Mosque
description: A mosque completed in 1902 in A‘dhamiyya by the merchant Shabandar family.

name: Fattah Pasha Mosque
description: A congregational mosque in Kadhimiya built in the royal era by the sons of the Turkmen statesman Fattah Pasha.

name: Al-Shawy Mosque
description: A 1957 mosque in Karkh inaugurated in the presence of King Faisal II, noted for calligraphy by Hashem Muhammad al-Baghdadi.

name: Ibn Bunnieh Mosque
description: A modern Iraqi mosque with an egg-shaped dome and calligraphy by Hashem Muhammad al-Baghdadi, opposite Baghdad Central Station.

name: Umm al-Tabul Mosque
description: A large mosque commemorating officers of the 1959 Mosul uprising, modelled on Cairo’s Citadel mosques.

name: Mosque of Salman al-Farsi
description: The tomb of Salman the Persian, companion of the Prophet, at Salman Pak, with a mosque established over the older mausoleum in 1950.

name: Baba Nanak Shrine
description: A Sikh shrine marking where Guru Nanak stayed outside Baghdad around 1511; rediscovered and rebuilt by Sikh soldiers in the two world wars, it survived in fair shape until 2003.

name: Khan Mirjan
description: A 14th-century caravanserai built by the Jalayirid governor Amin al-Din Mirjan, with a 13 m-high vaulted hall of brick arches; restored in the 1980s.

name: Souk al-Safafeer
description: The coppersmiths’ market off al-Rashid Street, active since the Abbasid period and linked to the Mustansiriya madrasa; its craft is now in decline.

sources.sourceName: Al Jazeera, 7 August 2018 — Baghdad’s coppersmith souk: a fading cultural treasure

name: Shorja Market
description: One of Baghdad’s historic marketplaces, with late-Abbasid origins, stretching from al-Kifah Street to the Mirjan mosque.

name: Al-Mutanabbi Street
description: The historic centre of Baghdad bookselling off al-Rashid Street, a gathering place of writers and intellectuals.

name: Al-Rashid Street
description: Baghdad’s first modern avenue, opened in 1916, lined with arcaded late-Ottoman and royal-era buildings and now a municipal conservation focus.

name: Al-Maidan Square
description: An old square from Bab al-Mu‘adham to al-Rashid Street with mosques, markets and the houses of royal-era politicians such as Nuri al-Said.

name: Bab al-Sheikh Quarter
description: An old Rusafa quarter around the Qadiriyya shrine, rich in Sufi lodges, tombs and mosques.

name: Bataween (former Jewish quarter)
description: A 1930s riverside quarter built by Iraqi Jews and Armenians, once home to synagogues, churches, schools and clubs, and the main Jewish quarter until the community left.

name: Sourp Asdvadzadzin Church (Miskinta)
description: Baghdad’s oldest church still in use, built in 1639–40 by an Armenian artillery officer of Sultan Murad IV after the conquest of Baghdad; rebuilt several times, last in 1967–70.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The church Sourp Asdvadzadzin in Baghdad

name: Om al-Ahzan Church (Mary Mother of Sorrows)
description: The old Chaldean patriarchal cathedral in Aqd al-Nasara, the historic Christian quarter of Shorja; built in 1843 and rebuilt 5 m higher in 1889 after floods, consecrated in 1898.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Church of Mary mother of sorrows in Baghdad
Wikipedia — Cathedral of Our Lady of Sorrows

name: Latin Church of St Joseph
description: The Carmelite church consecrated in 1871, long the Latin cathedral, with a 32 m dome visible across the old Christian quarter; requisitioned by Ottoman forces in 1917.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Mar Youssef latin church in Baghdad
Wikipedia — Latin Cathedral of St. Joseph

name: Syriac Catholic Church of the Immaculate Conception (site)
description: A church completed in 1862 next to Om al-Ahzan; abandoned when its community moved to Karrada and demolished at the end of 2018, 156 years after it opened.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The syriac-catholic church of our Lady of the Immaculate in Baghdad

name: Armenian Catholic Church of the Sacred Heart
description: A western-style brick basilica in Karrada consecrated in 1938, funded by the Kasparkhan sisters.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Armenian Catholic church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in Baghdad

name: Sourp Krikor Loussavoritch Armenian Cathedral
description: The Armenian Apostolic cathedral of 1954–57 with an octagonal cupola, on an estate holding an Armenian cemetery since 1904.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Armenian Apostolic Cathedral of Sourp Krikor Loussavoritch in Baghdad

name: Chaldean Cathedral of St Joseph, Karrada
description: The Chaldean cathedral begun in 1952 and consecrated in 1956, built when the community left Aqd al-Nasara for Karrada.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mar Yousef (St Joseph) cathedral in Baghdad
Wikipedia — Chaldean Cathedral of St. Joseph

name: Chaldean Church of Our Lady Queen of the Rosary
description: A domed church inaugurated in 1960 in Karrada, also called the church of Saint Rita.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Chaldean our Lady Queen of the Rosary church in Baghdad

name: Syriac Orthodox Cathedral of St Peter and St Paul
description: A large cathedral consecrated in 1964 by Patriarch Ignatius Yacoub III, twice targeted by car bombs after 2003.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — St Peter and St Paul Cathedral in Baghdad

name: Sayidat al-Nejat Cathedral
description: The Syriac Catholic cathedral of 1968 in Karrada where 47 worshippers were killed in the attack of 31 October 2010.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Cathedral Sayidat al Najat in Baghdad

name: Mar Gorgis Chaldean Church, New Baghdad
description: A church of 1969 in brick and concrete with a reverse arch and radiating apse, richly decorated with paintings, mosaics and stained glass.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Mar Gorgis Chaldean Church in Baghdad

review_notes: Source coordinates are garbled; no pin.

name: Great Synagogue of Baghdad (Shaf ve-Yativ)
description: A synagogue traditionally on the site of one founded by the exiled King Jeconiah; rebuilt several times and now a Jewish museum.

name: Meir Taweig Synagogue
description: A 1942 synagogue complex with school, library and community centre in Bataween, one of the city’s last.

name: Shamash School
description: A Jewish high school founded on al-Rashid Street in 1928 with Anglo-Jewish support; after 1950 it passed through other uses and stood as a garage before reopening as a heritage site.

name: Al-Habibiyah Jewish Cemetery
description: Baghdad’s Jewish cemetery near Sadr City with more than 4,000 graves, moved here in 1975 from the old cemetery in al-Nahda.

name: Baghdadi Museum
description: A folk museum opened in 1970 in a riverside building of 1869, with 70 life-size scenes of Baghdad crafts and street life.

name: Abd al-Karim Qasim Museum
description: A museum to Iraq’s first republican leader in a heritage house on al-Rashid Street.

name: Iraq Museum
description: The national museum, founded after the First World War to keep excavated finds in Iraq; looted in 2003 and reopened in 2015.

name: White Palace (al-Qasr al-Abyadh)
description: A domed royal guest house of 1934, built at King Ghazi’s order, where foreign heads of government were received.

name: Al-Rehab Palace
description: The private residence of the Iraqi royal family from 1937 to 1958, the last home of the monarchy.

name: Republican Palace
description: The third royal palace of the Hashemite kingdom, ordered by Faisal II and finished in the early 1960s; seat of the presidency from 1963 to 2003.

name: Royal Mausoleum (Iraqi Royal Cemetery)
description: The blue-domed mausoleum of the Iraqi royal family in A‘dhamiyya, designed by J. Brian Cooper and built in 1934–36 in Islamic style.

name: Baghdad Central Station
description: The domed main railway station designed by J. M. Wilson and built in 1948–53, described by the BBC as the “crown jewel” of Baghdad.

name: Al-Markaziyya High School
description: Iraq’s oldest and most renowned high school, founded in 1918.

name: University of Baghdad Campus (Gropius)
description: The Jadiriya campus planned by Walter Gropius and The Architects Collaborative, only partly built; its faculty office tower is among the surviving elements.

sources.sourceName: Monocle — How Le Corbusier and Walter Gropius built modernist Baghdad

name: Baghdad Gymnasium (Le Corbusier)
description: The only built part of the sports complex Le Corbusier designed from 1956 for King Faisal II; completed long after his death.

name: Al-Sarafiya Bridge
description: A steel truss bridge of the 1940s–50s linking Waziriyah and Utafiyah, damaged in 1991, partly destroyed by a truck bomb in 2007 and rebuilt in 2008.

name: Baghdad (North Gate) War Cemetery
description: A Commonwealth war cemetery with 4,480 burials and commemorations of both world wars, including 100 Turkish graves; repaired in 2012.

name: Freedom Monument (Nasb al-Hurriyah)
description: Jawad Saleem’s 1961 bronze frieze on a travertine wall in Tahrir Square, telling the story of the 14 July Revolution in a language drawn from ancient Mesopotamian art.

name: Kahramana Fountain
description: Mohammed Ghani Hikmat’s 1971 fountain of Marjana pouring oil on the forty thieves, one of Baghdad’s best-known public artworks.

name: Al-Shaheed Monument
description: Ismail Fatah al-Turk’s split turquoise dome of 1983 commemorating the dead of the Iran–Iraq War.

name: Monument to the Unknown Soldier
description: A monument built in 1979–82 by the Italian architect Marcello D’Olivo after a concept by Khaled al-Rahal.

sources.sourceName: Wikipedia — Monument to the Unknown Soldier, Baghdad

name: Victory Arch (Swords of Qadisiyah)
description: Twin arches of hands holding crossed swords marking the entrances to the Grand Festivities Square, opened in 1989.
